docs.title: 1. WHAT THIS SECTION IS SAYING
docs.text:
The Preview controls section is about what happens when you use:

mkdocs serve

In other words:

How does MkDocs behave while you're developing and previewing your documentation locally?

The settings here control things such as:

  • what directories MkDocs watches for changes
  • what URL structure the generated site uses
  • whether warnings stop the build
  • what local address the development server uses

Live Reloading

Navs for 3.1 Go back to Park I

docs.title: What MkDocs is saying
docs.text:
watch tells MkDocs about additional directories that it should monitor for changes when you run:

mkdocs serve

It is a YAML list.

watch:
  - directory_a
  - directory_b

Normally MkDocs watches the relevant project files automatically.

watch lets you add more directories to that set.

docs.title: Why would you need this?
docs.text:
Suppose you have files outside the normal locations that affect your documentation.

You can tell MkDocs:

“Also watch these directories. If something changes there, reload the preview.”

Instead of having to specify:

mkdocs serve -w directory_a -w directory_b

every time, you can put the directories in mkdocs.yml.

docs.title: Important path distinction
docs.text: There are two different ways of specifying watch paths.

docs.title: In mkdocs.yml
docs.text:
watch:
  - directory_a

The path is relative to the configuration file.

docs.title: On the command line
docs.text:
mkdocs serve --watch directory_a

The CLI-provided path is not relative to the configuration file.

This distinction is specifically called out by MkDocs.

So:

Configuration-file watch path
        ↓
relative to mkdocs.yml

CLI --watch path
        ↓
not relative to mkdocs.yml

docs.title: use_directory_urls
docs.text:
This setting controls the directory structure of the generated site and therefore the URL format used to link to pages.

There are two modes:

false
true

The difference is significant.

docs.title: use_directory_urls: false
docs.text:
This mode is useful when the hosting system cannot serve X/index.html when the URL is simply X.

When set to false, MkDocs doesn't create a directory containing index.html for each page.

Instead, it creates an .html file directly.

For example:

Source                 Generated file          URL

index.md               index.html              /index.html

api-guide.md           api-guide.html          /api-guide.html

about/license.md       about/license.html      /about/license.html

So:

api-guide.md
    ↓
api-guide.html
    ↓
/api-guide.html

rather than:

api-guide.md
    ↓
api-guide/index.html
    ↓
/api-guide/

docs.title: Why might you need this?
docs.text:
MkDocs specifically gives examples such as:

  • opening documentation pages directly from the filesystem
  • publishing documentation to a static S3 website

So if your hosting environment requires direct file access, false can be appropriate.

docs.title: use_directory_urls: true
docs.text:
This is the default.

Instead of making the URL point directly to an .html file, MkDocs organizes pages into directories containing:

index.html

For example:

Source                 Generated file              URL

index.md               /index.html                 /

api-guide.md           /api-guide/index.html       /api-guide/

about/license.md       /about/license/index.html   /about/license

The important transformation is:

api-guide.md
     ↓
api-guide/index.html
     ↓
/api-guide/

This produces what MkDocs describes as more user-friendly URLs.

docs.title: Default
docs.text: use_directory_urls: true

docs.title: The fundamental difference
docs.text: Think of the two modes like this:

docs.title: false
docs.text:
Markdown
   ↓
HTML FILE
   ↓
URL points to FILE

docs.title: true
docs.text:
Markdown
   ↓
directory/index.html
   ↓
URL points to DIRECTORY

So this setting isn't about whether MkDocs generates HTML.

Both modes generate HTML.

It is about how the generated HTML files are organized and how their URLs are exposed.

docs.title: strict
docs.text:
strict controls how MkDocs handles warnings.

strict: true

means:

If MkDocs raises a warning, stop processing.

strict: false

means:

Print the warning, but continue processing.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Imagine MkDocs finds a broken link.

With:

strict: false

you might get:

warning
    ↓
display warning
    ↓
continue

With:

strict: true

you get:

warning
    ↓
treated as fatal
    ↓
processing stops

There is also a command-line equivalent:

mkdocs build --strict

docs.title: Default
docs.text:
strict: false

docs.title: dev_addr
docs.text:
dev_addr specifies the address used by:

mkdocs serve

It must have this format:

IP:PORT

The default is:

127.0.0.1:8000

So MkDocs' development server normally runs at:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/

You can configure a different default:

dev_addr: 127.0.0.1:9000

This saves you from having to provide:

--dev-addr

every time you run mkdocs serve.

docs.title: Default
docs.text: dev_addr: '127.0.0.1:8000'

docs.title: 1. WHAT THIS SECTION IS SAYING
docs.text:
Now MkDocs moves from:

How do I preview my site?

to:

How does MkDocs process and extend my Markdown when building the site?

The three major configuration areas here are:

markdown_extensions
hooks
plugins

They operate at different levels.

A useful high-level picture is:

Markdown files
      │
      ↓
Python-Markdown
      │
      ├── markdown_extensions
      │
      ↓
MkDocs processing
      │
      ├── hooks
      │
      └── plugins
      │
      ↓
generated HTML/site

docs.title: markdown_extensions
docs.text:
MkDocs uses the Python Markdown library to convert Markdown files into HTML.

So the basic pipeline is:

Markdown
   ↓
Python Markdown
   ↓
HTML

Python Markdown has extensions that change or add to how Markdown is interpreted.

MkDocs lets you enable those extensions using:

markdown_extensions:

MkDocs itself uses these extensions by default:

meta
toc
tables
fenced_code

You can add more.

docs.title: Enabling an extension
docs.text:
For example, to enable the Python Markdown SmartyPants typography extension:

markdown_extensions:
  - smarty

This means:

markdown_extensions
       ↓
     smarty
       ↓
enable this Markdown extension

docs.title: Default
docs.text:
markdown_extensions: []

The displayed default is an empty list because this setting represents additional extensions you configure; MkDocs still has its own built-in/default extensions.

docs.title: Extensions can have their own configuration
docs.text:
An extension may expose its own settings.

For example, the built-in toc extension supports:

permalink

You can configure it like this:

markdown_extensions:
  - toc:
      permalink: true

Notice the YAML structure:

- toc:
    permalink: true

The colon after:

toc:

turns toc into a mapping whose value contains another mapping.

docs.title: Multiple options
docs.text:
An extension can have several options:

markdown_extensions:
  - toc:
      permalink: true
      separator: "_"

Each option gets its own line and indentation.

Conceptually:

toc
├── permalink → true
└── separator → "_"

docs.title: Multiple extensions
docs.text:
You add another list item for each extension:

markdown_extensions:
  - smarty
  - toc:
      permalink: true
  - sane_lists

So:

- smarty
      ↓
extension with no custom options

- toc:
    permalink: true
      ↓
extension with configuration

- sane_lists
      ↓
another extension with no custom options

docs.title: Dynamic configuration values
docs.text:
MkDocs allows extension configuration values to be obtained dynamically.

The documentation points to two mechanisms:

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Values can come from environment variables.

docs.title: Current paths
docs.text:
Values can use paths associated with:

  • the Markdown file currently being rendered
  • the overall MkDocs site

These capabilities are covered elsewhere in the Configuration documentation.

docs.title: Alternative syntax for extensions
docs.text:
Instead of representing extensions as list items:

markdown_extensions:
  - smarty
  - toc:
      permalink: true
  - sane_lists

you can represent them as key/value pairs:

markdown_extensions:
  smarty: {}
  toc:
    permalink: true
  sane_lists: {}

There is one important difference.

For an extension with no options, you must explicitly provide an empty value:

smarty: {}

rather than simply:

smarty:

The {} represents an empty mapping.

docs.title: Why does MkDocs mention this alternative syntax?
docs.text:
Because it becomes required when using configuration inheritance and you want to override options in inherited configurations.

So this isn't merely two interchangeable styles for aesthetic reasons.

The alternative mapping syntax has a specific practical use later in the configuration system.

docs.title: More extensions
docs.text:
Python Markdown provides many extensions that can be used without installing something separately.

There are also third-party extensions.

MkDocs points users toward:

  • Python Markdown's extension documentation
  • the Python Markdown third-party extension ecosystem
  • the MkDocs project catalog

Third-party extensions may have their own installation procedures and configuration options.

The key point is:

Python Markdown
       ↓
built-in extensions
       +
third-party extensions
       ↓
customize Markdown processing

docs.title: hooks
docs.text:
New in MkDocs 1.4

hooks lets you specify Python scripts that MkDocs loads and uses as plugin instances.

Example:

hooks:
  - my_hooks.py

The path is relative to:

mkdocs.yml

The Python file can contain plugin event handlers.

For example:

def on_page_markdown(markdown, **kwargs):
    return markdown.replace('a', 'z')

This function runs when MkDocs processes page Markdown and returns modified Markdown.

docs.title: What is a hook actually doing?
docs.text:
The important conceptual model is:

MkDocs event
     ↓
hook function
     ↓
your custom Python logic
     ↓
result returned to MkDocs

For example:

Markdown
   ↓
on_page_markdown()
   ↓
modify Markdown
   ↓
MkDocs continues processing

docs.title: Advanced hook example
docs.text:
MkDocs gives an example where a hook scans Markdown for non-HTTPS links and generates warnings.

The script:

import logging, re
import mkdocs.plugins

log = logging.getLogger('mkdocs')

@mkdocs.plugins.event_priority(-50)
def on_page_markdown(markdown, page, **kwargs):
    path = page.file.src_uri
    for m in re.finditer(r'\bhttp://[^) ]+', markdown):
        log.warning(f"Documentation file '{path}' contains a non-HTTPS link: {m[0]}')

The important idea isn't memorizing the Python.

The hook:

reads Markdown
    ↓
looks for http:// links
    ↓
logs a warning

And because warnings can become fatal under:

mkdocs build --strict

this can effectively turn the hook into a documentation-quality check.

docs.title: Hooks versus plugins
docs.text:
MkDocs explicitly says hooks don't provide new capabilities compared with plugins.

Instead, hooks simplify one-off uses.

A plugin generally needs to be installed as a plugin package.

A hook can simply be a Python file in your project.

So:

plugin
   ↓
reusable/installed extension mechanism

hook
   ↓
simple project-local customization

The hook system is therefore particularly convenient when you need a small piece of custom behavior for one project.

docs.title: mkdocs-simple-hooks
docs.text:
The documentation notes that this functionality may look familiar if you've used the:

mkdocs-simple-hooks

plugin.

A configuration using that plugin can sometimes be replaced directly with the built-in hooks configuration.

Old:

plugins:
  - mkdocs-simple-hooks:
      hooks:
        on_page_markdown: 'my_hooks:on_page_markdown'

New:

hooks:
  - my_hooks.py

docs.title: Important mkdocs serve behavior
docs.text:
When using:

mkdocs serve

the hook module is not reloaded on every build.

That's an important development-time caveat.

Changes to the hook itself therefore don't necessarily behave like changes to ordinary watched documentation content.

docs.title: MkDocs 1.6 — adjacent imports
docs.text:
MkDocs 1.6 made another improvement.

If the hook file has another Python file next to it:

hooks/
├── my_hooks.py
└── foo.py

the hook can use normal Python syntax:

import foo

to access functions from foo.py.

Older versions required a workaround involving:

sys.path

docs.title: plugins
docs.text:
plugins specifies the plugins MkDocs should use when building the site.

It is a YAML list, and each plugin can optionally have its own configuration.

docs.title: Default
docs.text:
MkDocs provides:

search

by default.

So conceptually:

plugins:
  - search

is the default plugin configuration.

docs.title: Important behavior when you define plugins
docs.text:
This is a major MkDocs configuration rule.

If you explicitly define:

plugins:

you replace the default plugin configuration.

You don't merely add to it.

Therefore, if you write:

plugins:
  - your_other_plugin

you have removed the default:

search

plugin unless you explicitly add it back.

So:

plugins:
  - search
  - your_other_plugin

means:

keep search
+
add your plugin

docs.title: Disabling all plugins
docs.text:
To completely disable plugins:

plugins: []

This also disables the default search plugin.

docs.title: Configuring a plugin
docs.text:
A plugin can have its own options.

For example:

plugins:
  - search
  - your_other_plugin:
      option1: value
      option2: other value

The structure is:

plugin
   ↓
configuration mapping
   ↓
individual plugin options

docs.title: enabled
docs.text:
New in MkDocs 1.6

Every plugin has an enabled Boolean option supplied by MkDocs.

This lets you conditionally enable or disable a plugin.

For example:

plugins:
  - search
  - code-validator:
      enabled: !ENV [LINT, false]

Here enabled receives a value from an environment variable through the !ENV YAML tag.

So the conceptual chain is:

environment variable
        ↓
      !ENV
        ↓
     enabled
        ↓
 plugin on/off

docs.title: Alternate plugin syntax
docs.text:
Plugins can also use mapping syntax rather than list syntax.

Instead of:

plugins:
  - search
  - your_other_plugin:
      option1: value
      option2: other value

you can write:

plugins:
  search: {}
  your_other_plugin:
    option1: value
    option2: other value

Again, the plugin with no options needs:

{}

The documentation specifically says this alternative syntax is required for configuration inheritance when overriding plugin options.

docs.title: Search plugin
docs.text:
MkDocs includes a Search plugin by default.

It uses:

Lunr.js

as its search engine.

The available settings control how MkDocs builds and uses the search index.

Those settings are:

separator
min_search_length
lang
prebuild_index
indexing

docs.title: separator
docs.text:
separator is a regular expression that tells the search indexer which characters should be treated as word separators.

The default is:

[\s\-]+

This means whitespace and hyphens are treated as separators.

For example, you could add the dot:

plugins:
  - search:
      separator: '[\s\-\.]+'

Now the dot is also treated as a word separator.

docs.title: Default
docs.text: [\s\-]+

docs.title: min_search_length
docs.text:
This is an integer specifying the minimum number of characters a search query must contain.

The default is:

3

So searches shorter than three characters are ignored.

Why?

MkDocs says short search terms generally produce poor-quality search results.

But there are legitimate cases where short terms matter.

For example, documentation about Message Queues might naturally involve:

MQ

which is only two characters.

You could therefore configure:

plugins:
  - search:
      min_search_length: 2

docs.title: Default
docs.text: 3

docs.title: lang
docs.text:
lang specifies the languages used when building the search index.

Languages are identified using ISO 639-1 language codes.

For example:

en → English
fr → French
de → German
ja → Japanese

MkDocs/Lunr Languages supports the listed languages:

ar  Arabic
da  Danish
nl  Dutch
en  English
fi  Finnish
fr  French
de  German
hu  Hungarian
it  Italian
ja  Japanese
no  Norwegian
pt  Portuguese
ro  Romanian
ru  Russian
es  Spanish
sv  Swedish
th  Thai
tr  Turkish
vi  Vietnamese

You can configure multiple languages.

docs.title: Why not just add every language?
docs.text:
MkDocs warns against doing that unless you actually need them.

Each additional language increases:

  • bandwidth requirements
  • browser resource usage

The documentation therefore recommends generally keeping each MkDocs instance to a single language.

docs.title: Chinese and other Asian languages
docs.text:
The documentation notes that Lunr Languages does not currently include support for Chinese or some other Asian languages.

It says some users have reported decent results with Japanese.

That is a limitation of the search-language support, not a general statement about whether MkDocs can contain Chinese documentation.

docs.title: Default language
docs.text:
The default value is:

theme.locale

if you've configured theme.locale.

Otherwise:

[en]

So:

theme.locale
      ↓
search language

when a locale is explicitly set.

docs.title: prebuild_index
docs.text:
This optionally generates a pre-built search index containing the site's pages.

The purpose is performance.

It can improve search performance on larger sites.

Set:

plugins:
  - search:
      prebuild_index: true

to enable it.

But the documentation says to first make sure your theme explicitly supports a prebuilt index. The built-in themes do.

docs.title: Node.js requirement
docs.text:
This option requires:

Node.js

to be installed, with:

node

available on the system path.

If MkDocs tries to call Node.js and it fails:

warning
   ↓
build continues

rather than automatically stopping.

However, if you use:

--strict

the warning can become an error.

docs.title: Small site versus large site
docs.text:
The documentation makes an important performance distinction.

For smaller sites, a pre-built index isn't recommended because:

more bandwidth
      +
little/no noticeable benefit

For large sites—particularly hundreds of pages—the tradeoff can make more sense:

larger index/bandwidth cost
      +
significant search-performance improvement

docs.title: indexing
docs.text:
indexing controls how much content the search index contains.

Example:

plugins:
  - search:
      indexing: 'full'

There are three options.

Setting What gets indexed full Title + section headings + full page text sections Title + section headings titles Title only

So:

full
 ↓
maximum searchable content

sections
 ↓
title + headings

titles
 ↓
title only

The documentation notes that this is particularly useful for large projects where the search index itself becomes very large and consumes significant disk space.

docs.title: 2. OFFICIAL TERMINOLOGY — FORMATTING OPTIONS
docs.text: Term Meaning Markdown processor Software that converts Markdown into another format, here HTML Python Markdown The Markdown-processing library MkDocs uses extension An add-on that changes or expands Markdown processing plugin An MkDocs component that hooks into the build process to provide functionality hook Project-local Python code that responds to MkDocs events event Something occurring during MkDocs' processing lifecycle event handler A function that runs when a particular event occurs mapping YAML collection of key/value pairs empty mapping {}; a mapping containing no key/value pairs environment variable A value supplied by the operating system/environment dynamic configuration Configuration whose value can be supplied or resolved at runtime/build time regular expression A pattern language used to find/match text search index Data structure allowing a search system to find content efficiently indexer Component that creates the search index pre-built index A search index generated in advance rather than built in the browser bandwidth Amount of data transferred over a network browser resources CPU, memory, network and related resources used by the browser locale Language/region setting ISO 639-1 Standard using two-letter codes to identify languages third-party extension Extension developed outside the core project one-off Something intended for a particular project/use rather than a reusable installed component conditional Behavior that depends on whether a condition/value is true or false

docs.title: Extension list syntax
docs.text:
markdown_extensions:
  - smarty

The - means:

This is one item in the list.

docs.title: Extension with options
docs.text:
markdown_extensions:
  - toc:
      permalink: true

The structure is:

list
 ↓
toc
 ↓
mapping of options
 ↓
permalink: true

docs.title: Mapping syntax
docs.text:
markdown_extensions:
  toc:
    permalink: true

This is structurally different from the list form.

The empty mapping:

smarty: {}

means:

smarty is configured, but has no options.

docs.title: Plugin configuration
docs.text:
plugins:
  - search:
      min_search_length: 2

means:

plugins
  ↓
search plugin
  ↓
min_search_length
  ↓
2

docs.title: Regular expression
docs.text:
[\s\-\.]+

You don't need to memorize the individual regex symbols from this page yet.

For MST purposes, the important meaning is:

This is a pattern that tells the search system which characters count as word separators.

docs.title: Search indexing levels
docs.text:
full
sections
titles

These aren't YAML types; they're allowed values for the indexing configuration option.

docs.title: 4. HOW THE PIECES CONNECT
docs.text: The Formatting options section has three different extension mechanisms.

docs.title: Markdown extensions
docs.text:
Markdown
   ↓
Python Markdown
   ↓
markdown_extensions
   ↓
how Markdown is interpreted/formatted

These primarily affect Markdown processing.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
MkDocs event
     ↓
hooks
     ↓
your Python function
     ↓
custom action

These let you insert project-local Python logic into MkDocs' processing events.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
MkDocs build
     ↓
plugins
     ↓
additional functionality

Plugins are the more general MkDocs extension mechanism.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
The built-in Search plugin then has its own configuration:

plugins
   ↓
search
   │
   ├── separator
   │
   ├── min_search_length
   │
   ├── lang
   │
   ├── prebuild_index
   │
   └── indexing

So don't mentally treat these as six independent MkDocs systems.

They are options belonging to the Search plugin.

docs.title: 🔴 Must understand
docs.text:
The important conceptual distinctions are:

watch
↓
what MkDocs watches during serve

use_directory_urls
↓
how generated pages are organized/exposed through URLs

strict
↓
whether warnings stop processing

dev_addr
↓
where the local development server runs

And:

markdown_extensions
↓
customize Markdown processing

hooks
↓
project-local Python event handlers

plugins
↓
MkDocs functionality/extensions

For plugins, this behavior is particularly important:

Don't define plugins
       ↓
MkDocs gets default search plugin

Define plugins:
       ↓
defaults are replaced
       ↓
explicitly add search if you still want it

And understand the two plugin/extension configuration styles:

# List style
- search

versus:

# Mapping style
search: {}

The latter becomes important for inheritance.

For Search itself, understand:

separator
↓
what counts as a word boundary

min_search_length
↓
shortest accepted search query

lang
↓
languages used for search

prebuild_index
↓
whether a search index is generated ahead of time

indexing
↓
how much page content enters the search index

docs.text:
PREVIEW CONTROLS
       ↓
How does MkDocs behave while I am developing/previewing?

             ↓

FORMATTING OPTIONS
       ↓
How does MkDocs process Markdown
and extend the build with additional functionality?

And one especially useful distinction from these two sections:

markdown_extensions
        ↓

That distinction will become useful later when you encounter more advanced Docs-as-Code configurations.

**TOPSIES

docs.title: Nav and Theme 2
docs.text:
nav and theme are not two flat lists of settings. They are two different configuration structures with different grammars.

So let's treat them like a language.

docs.title: 1. The "alphabet" of nav
docs.text:
Core MkDocs nav has a surprisingly small fundamental grammar. The official MkDocs configuration reference confirms that nav defines the format/layout of global navigation, with internal pages, nested sections, and external links. (MkDocs)

At its simplest:

nav:
  - item
  - item
  - item

nav is a YAML sequence.

An item can fundamentally be:

docs.title: A. A page
docs.text: - Home: index.md

docs.title: B. A section containing more items
docs.text:
- Guides:
    - Installation: installation.md
    - Configuration: configuration.md

docs.title: C. An external link
docs.text:
- MkDocs: https://www.mkdocs.org/

And those can recursively contain one another.

That's the grammar.

docs.title: 2. Think of nav as a recursive language
docs.text:
This is the part that was missing.

Conceptually:

NAV
│
└── ITEM
     │
     ├── PAGE
     │    ├── label → file
     │    └── file
     │
     ├── SECTION
     │    └── ITEM
     │         └── ITEM
     │              └── ...
     │
     └── LINK
          ├── label
          └── URL

So:

nav:
  - Home: index.md

is:

NAV
└── PAGE

While:

nav:
  - Guides:
      - Installation: installation.md
      - Configuration: configuration.md

is:

NAV
└── SECTION
    ├── PAGE
    └── PAGE

And:

nav:
  - Guides:
      - Configuration:
          - YAML: yaml.md
          - Markdown: markdown.md

is:

NAV
└── SECTION
    └── SECTION
        ├── PAGE
        └── PAGE

That's the mechanism.

You're not memorizing a "nav tree."

You're learning a structure in which a section can contain navigation items, and those items can themselves be sections.

docs.title: 3. Now you can generate your own nav
docs.text:
Once you understand that grammar, you can invent this:

nav:
  - Home: index.md

  - Learn:
      - Markdown: markdown.md
      - YAML:
          - Scalars: yaml/scalars.md
          - Sequences: yaml/sequences.md
          - Mappings: yaml/mappings.md

  - Projects:
      - Project A:
          - Overview: projects/a/index.md
          - Setup: projects/a/setup.md
      - Project B:
          - Overview: projects/b/index.md
          - Reference: projects/b/reference.md

  - External:
      - MkDocs: https://www.mkdocs.org/
      - Material: https://squidfunk.github.io/mkdocs-material/

You didn't memorize that configuration.

You generated it from the grammar.

That is what you were asking for.

docs.title: 4. theme is fundamentally different
docs.text:
Now we get to the more complicated one.

Core MkDocs defines:

theme:

as a configuration object that selects a theme and passes theme-specific configuration to it. MkDocs itself defines things such as name, locale, custom_dir, and static_templates; additional keys belong to the selected theme. (MkDocs)

So:

theme:
  name: material

means:

THEME
│
└── NAME
    └── MATERIAL

But once you say:

name: material

you're effectively saying:

"The rest of the vocabulary inside this theme: object can now include Material's vocabulary."

That's why theme cannot have one universal list of children.

docs.title: 5. The actual architecture
docs.text:
Think of it like this:

mkdocs.yml
│
├── NAV
│
│   └── MkDocs defines the grammar
│
└── THEME
    │
    ├── MkDocs defines the theme interface
    │
    └── selected theme
         │
         └── Material
              │
              └── Material defines additional vocabulary

This is explicitly how MkDocs describes it: theme-specific keywords are allowed under theme, and you consult the documentation for the theme you're using. (MkDocs)

So asking:

"What are all the possible children of theme?"

has two answers:

docs.title: Core MkDocs
docs.text:
theme:
  name:
  locale:
  custom_dir:
  static_templates:

docs.title: Material
docs.text: Then Material adds its own configuration vocabulary.

docs.title: 6. Now let's map Material's vocabulary
docs.text:
Material's current documentation organizes its customization into areas including navigation, colors, fonts, logo/icons, search, header, footer, analytics, repository integration, and more. (GitHub Pages)

A useful structural map is:

theme:
│
├── name
│
├── palette
│   ├── scheme
│   ├── primary
│   ├── accent
│   ├── toggle
│   └── media
│
├── font
│   ├── text
│   └── code
│
├── logo
│
├── favicon
│
├── icon
│   ├── logo
│   ├── repo
│   ├── alternate
│   ├── previous
│   ├── next
│   └── ...
│
└── features
    └── FEATURE FLAGS

But there is an important qualification: Material's configuration surface is larger than this simplified map, and some behavior is configured outside theme, such as extra, Markdown extensions, plugins, CSS, and JavaScript. The Material documentation's setup/reference is therefore the actual authoritative catalogue. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: 7. palette — now let's REALLY explain it
docs.text:
Your original example:

theme:
  name: material
  palette:
    scheme: default
    primary: blue

Let's parse it mechanically.

theme
│
└── palette

palette is a mapping.

Inside it:

palette
│
├── scheme
│
├── primary
│
└── accent

Those are different properties.

Material currently documents two color schemes:

default → light
slate   → dark

and separate primary and accent color settings. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: 8. primary is not a YAML concept
docs.text:
This is another crucial distinction.

YAML doesn't know what this means:

primary: blue

YAML merely understands:

KEY → VALUE

Material gives the key primary its meaning.

So:

primary: blue

means:

Material's property:
primary

Value:
blue

Material then interprets blue as one of its supported color names.

Material's primary color affects things such as the header, sidebar, text links and other interface components. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: 9. What values can primary accept?
docs.text:
This is exactly the "alphabet" you're asking for.

Material's documented predefined color palette includes names such as:

red
pink
purple
deep purple
indigo
blue
light blue
cyan
teal
green
light green
lime
yellow
amber
orange
deep orange
brown
grey
blue grey
black
white

The available choices depend on the particular property; Material documents the primary and accent palettes separately. (GitHub Pages)

So:

primary: blue

is legal.

And:

primary: deep purple

is also legal.

But:

primary: banana

is not a Material predefined color.

That's the kind of information a configuration reference should give you.

docs.title: 10. accent
docs.text:
Material also has:

accent: orange

So:

palette:
  primary: blue
  accent: orange

means:

palette
│
├── primary → blue
│
└── accent → orange

Material uses the accent color for interactive/highlight elements. (GitHub Pages)

And no, Material doesn't have a standard:

secondary:

equivalent in this palette configuration.

docs.title: 11. scheme
docs.text:
Then:

scheme: default

is another key/value pair.

The value must be one of Material's supported schemes:

default
slate

So:

palette:
  scheme: slate

means:

Use the dark color scheme.

docs.title: 12. But then something fascinating happens
docs.text:
You can turn:

palette:
  scheme: default
  primary: blue

into:

palette:

  - scheme: default
    primary: blue
    accent: orange

  - scheme: slate
    primary: blue
    accent: orange

The YAML data type changed.

Before:

palette → mapping

After:

palette → sequence
              │
              ├── mapping
              └── mapping

Why?

Because Material interprets multiple palette entries as multiple selectable configurations. Its documentation explicitly shows the palette becoming a list when configuring a light/dark toggle. (GitHub Pages)

That is configuration grammar in action.

docs.title: 13. toggle belongs to a palette entry
docs.text:
For example:

palette:

  - scheme: default
    toggle:
      icon: material/brightness-7
      name: Switch to dark mode

  - scheme: slate
    toggle:
      icon: material/brightness-4
      name: Switch to light mode

Now the structure is:

palette
│
├── ITEM 1
│   ├── scheme
│   └── toggle
│       ├── icon
│       └── name
│
└── ITEM 2
    ├── scheme
    └── toggle
        ├── icon
        └── name

Material documents toggle as part of this palette configuration. (GitHub Pages)

Again, you're no longer memorizing snippets.

You're learning which object can contain which other objects.

docs.title: 14. Now features
docs.text:
This:

theme:
  features:
    - navigation.tabs
    - navigation.top

has a completely different grammar.

features is a sequence of strings.

Think:

features
│
├── "navigation.tabs"
└── "navigation.top"

Each string is a feature flag.

Material recognizes the feature names and activates the corresponding behavior.

For example:

- navigation.tabs

activates navigation tabs.

- navigation.sections

activates section grouping.

- navigation.expand

expands collapsible subsections by default.

- navigation.top

enables the back-to-top behavior.

- navigation.path

adds navigation breadcrumbs.

These are all documented Material feature flags. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: 15. And here's the entire navigation.* vocabulary
docs.text:
This is much closer to the thing you originally wanted.

Material currently documents navigation-related feature flags including:

navigation.instant
navigation.instant.prefetch
navigation.instant.progress
navigation.instant.preview

navigation.tracking

navigation.tabs
navigation.tabs.sticky

navigation.sections
navigation.expand

navigation.path
navigation.prune

navigation.indexes
navigation.top

navigation.footer

These aren't arbitrary words.

They are feature identifiers defined by Material. (GitHub Pages)

And they have relationships.

For example:

navigation.tabs
└── navigation.tabs.sticky

means:

sticky is a refinement of the tabs behavior.

Likewise:

navigation.instant
├── navigation.instant.prefetch
├── navigation.instant.progress
└── navigation.instant.preview

means the latter features extend the instant-navigation system. Material's documentation explicitly describes those relationships. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: 16. This is the distinction you kept asking me for
docs.text:
You don't need to think:

"What does navigation.tabs mean?"

in isolation.

You need to understand:

theme
└── features
    └── list of Material feature identifiers

Therefore:

theme:
  features:
    - navigation.tabs

is grammatically:

THEME
  contains FEATURES

FEATURES
  contains a LIST

LIST
  contains the VALUE "navigation.tabs"

Material then interprets that value as:

activate navigation tabs.

That's the mechanism.

docs.title: 17. nav and theme.features now fit together
docs.text:
Suppose you write:

nav:
  - Home: index.md

  - Guides:
      - Installation: install.md
      - Configuration: config.md

  - Reference:
      - YAML: yaml.md

That creates the information architecture:

Home
Guides
├── Installation
└── Configuration
Reference
└── YAML

Then:

theme:
  name: material
  features:
    - navigation.tabs
    - navigation.sections

does not create those pages.

It tells Material how to render the navigation structure you've already defined.

Material's documentation explicitly says navigation.tabs renders top-level sections as tabs and navigation.sections renders top-level sections as groups in the sidebar. (GitHub Pages)

So:

             nav
              │
              ▼
       WHAT EXISTS
              │
              ▼
        Navigation tree
              │
              │
              ▼
     Material features
              │
              ▼
       HOW IT APPEARS

That is the relationship.

docs.title: 18. And now you can invent your own site
docs.text:
For example:

site_name: My Documentation

nav:
  - Home: index.md

  - Tutorials:
      - Getting Started: tutorials/getting-started.md
      - MkDocs:
          - Navigation: tutorials/mkdocs-navigation.md
          - Themes: tutorials/mkdocs-themes.md

  - Reference:
      - Configuration: reference/configuration.md
      - Commands: reference/commands.md

theme:
  name: material

  palette:
    - scheme: default
      primary: indigo
      accent: amber
      toggle:
        icon: material/brightness-7
        name: Switch to dark mode

    - scheme: slate
      primary: indigo
      accent: amber
      toggle:
        icon: material/brightness-4
        name: Switch to light mode

  features:
    - navigation.tabs
    - navigation.sections
    - navigation.expand
    - navigation.top
    - navigation.path
    - navigation.footer

And now you can read every structural level:

site_name
└── scalar

nav
└── sequence
    ├── page
    ├── section
    │   ├── page
    │   └── section
    │       ├── page
    │       └── page
    └── section
        └── page

theme
└── mapping
    ├── name → scalar
    ├── palette → sequence
    │   ├── mapping
    │   └── mapping
    └── features → sequence
        ├── string
        ├── string
        └── string

THIS is the level of understanding you were asking for.

Not:

"Here's an example of navigation.tabs."

But:

What type of thing is navigation.tabs? Where can it legally occur? What contains it? What does the containing structure expect? What other members exist beside it? What values can those members take? What relationships exist between them?

That's the difference between copying configuration and speaking the configuration language.

And the official references are now useful in a completely different way: MkDocs Configuration gives you the core language, while Material's Setup/Reference gives you the Material vocabulary layered on top of it. (MkDocs)

If you want the literal A–Z treatment, the next step is to take nav and theme separately and build a configuration grammar/reference for each: every key → accepted value types → allowed children → what each value does → combinations → conflicts → working examples. That is the document you were asking for, rather than another tour of example sites.

docs.title: Nav & Theme
docs.text:
You're right about the problem: theme: name: material is not an explanation of theme; it is one example of a theme configuration. If your goal is to be able to construct and modify your own configuration, you need to understand the configuration grammar and the available keys, not memorize snippets.

I checked the current MkDocs documentation and the current Material for MkDocs documentation. The crucial thing is that nav and theme belong to two different configuration layers:

  • nav is a core MkDocs configuration setting.
  • theme is a core MkDocs configuration setting, but most of the things you put inside theme: are determined by the particular theme you're using. Material therefore has its own configuration vocabulary. (MkDocs)

Let's teach them from the ground up.

docs.title: 1. What nav actually is
docs.text:
nav is a YAML value assigned to the MkDocs configuration key nav.

Its job is:

Define the pages and hierarchy of the site's global navigation.

Officially, MkDocs describes it as determining the format and layout of the site's global navigation. (MkDocs)

So:

nav:

means:

"MkDocs, I'm going to explicitly tell you how I want my site's navigation organized."

It is not telling MkDocs where your files physically have to be.

This distinction is important.

You can have:

docs/
├── banana.md
├── apple.md
└── vegetables/
    └── carrot.md

and create:

nav:
  - Introduction: banana.md
  - Fruit: apple.md
  - Vegetables:
      - Carrots: vegetables/carrot.md

The navigation can have completely different names and organization from your filesystem.

docs.title: 2. The fundamental nav grammar
docs.text: There are essentially three things you need to understand:

docs.title: A. A page
docs.text: - Home: index.md

docs.title: B. A section
docs.text:
- Guides:
    - Getting Started: getting-started.md
    - Configuration: configuration.md

docs.title: C. An external link
docs.text:
- MkDocs: https://www.mkdocs.org/

That's the basic vocabulary.

docs.title: 3. Page entries
docs.text:
Consider:

nav:
  - Home: index.md
  - About: about.md

The syntax:

- Home: index.md

contains:

Home
 ↓
navigation title

index.md
 ↓
source Markdown file

The - means this is an item in a YAML sequence.

The : separates the key from the value.

So:

Home: index.md

is a YAML mapping.

You could write:

nav:
  - Introduction: index.md
  - My First Page: about.md
  - Whatever I Want: getting-started.md

The Markdown filenames don't change.

Only the navigation labels change.

MkDocs uses the title in nav as the page's title throughout the site when one is supplied. (MkDocs)

docs.title: 4. You don't actually have to provide the title
docs.text:
This is valid:

nav:
  - index.md
  - about.md

MkDocs can infer the page title.

Its title-resolution order is essentially:

  1. title supplied in nav
  2. page front matter title
  3. first level-1 Markdown heading
  4. filename (MkDocs)

So these are different:

- About: about.md

and:

- about.md

The first explicitly says:

Display this as About.

The second says:

MkDocs, figure out the title from the page.

docs.title: 5. Sections
docs.text:
Now we get to the thing people keep calling a navigation tree.

nav:
  - Home: index.md

  - Guides:
      - Getting Started: guides/getting-started.md
      - Configuration: guides/configuration.md

  - Reference:
      - YAML: reference/yaml.md
      - Markdown: reference/markdown.md

Conceptually:

Home

Guides
├── Getting Started
└── Configuration

Reference
├── YAML
└── Markdown

Guides isn't a Markdown file in this example.

It is a section/container.

MkDocs' terminology is important here:

A section contains child navigation items.

A section itself isn't inherently a page/link in core MkDocs. Sections can contain pages and further sections, and they can be nested as deeply as you like. (MkDocs)

docs.title: 6. You can nest sections
docs.text:
For example:

nav:
  - Guides:
      - Getting Started:
          - Installation: guides/install.md
          - First Project: guides/first-project.md

      - Configuration:
          - Basic: guides/config/basic.md
          - Advanced: guides/config/advanced.md

The resulting structure is:

Guides
│
├── Getting Started
│   ├── Installation
│   └── First Project
│
└── Configuration
    ├── Basic
    └── Advanced

This is what people mean by a navigation tree.

There is nothing magical happening.

It's simply nested YAML structures being interpreted as a hierarchy.

docs.title: 7. nav does NOT have a fixed maximum hierarchy
docs.text:
Core MkDocs allows sections to be nested arbitrarily deeply. (MkDocs)

So theoretically:

nav:
  - Level 1:
      - Level 2:
          - Level 3:
              - Level 4:
                  - Level 5:
                      - Page: page.md

is structurally possible.

Whether a particular theme displays that hierarchy nicely is a separate question.

That's one of the most important distinctions in this entire subject:

MKDOCS
│
├── understands your navigation structure
│
└── THEME
     └── decides how that structure is presented visually

docs.title: 8. nav does not equal your folders
docs.text:
Suppose:

docs/
├── index.md
├── stuff.md
├── banana.md
└── extremely-deep-folder/
    └── thing.md

You can make:

nav:
  - Home: index.md
  - My Important Stuff: stuff.md
  - Fruit: banana.md
  - Secret:
      - Thing: extremely-deep-folder/thing.md

The navigation hierarchy doesn't have to mirror the directory hierarchy.

The only requirement is that the paths you specify point to the appropriate files relative to your docs_dir. (MkDocs)

docs.title: 9. What happens if you don't use nav?
docs.text:
This is extremely important.

If you omit nav:

site_name: My Site

MkDocs automatically discovers Markdown files in your documentation directory and creates navigation from them.

The automatic navigation is ordered alphanumerically, with index files receiving special treatment. (MkDocs)

So:

docs/
├── index.md
├── apple.md
├── banana.md
└── carrot.md

can automatically produce something like:

Home
Apple
Banana
Carrot

When you add:

nav:

you're essentially saying:

Stop leaving this organization to automatic discovery; I want to explicitly define it.

docs.title: 10. Pages missing from nav
docs.text:
This is another subtle but important point.

Suppose:

docs/
├── index.md
├── guide.md
└── secret.md

but:

nav:
  - Home: index.md
  - Guide: guide.md

secret.md isn't necessarily deleted.

MkDocs can still build it.

It simply isn't connected to the global navigation.

The official documentation describes such pages as rendered but not linked from global navigation. (MkDocs)

So:

filesystem
    ≠
navigation

That's fundamental.

docs.title: PART II — theme
docs.text: Now let's deal with the thing that was bothering you.

docs.title: 11. What theme actually is
docs.text:
Core MkDocs defines:

theme:

as the configuration for:

which theme renders your documentation and how that theme is configured.

MkDocs itself provides built-in themes, while third-party themes provide their own additional configuration options. (MkDocs)

So this:

theme:
  name: material

contains two levels:

theme
└── name
    └── material

Meaning:

Use the installed theme named material.

docs.title: 12. Why theme becomes confusing
docs.text:
Because this:

theme:
  name: material
  palette:
    primary: blue

contains both MkDocs concepts and Material concepts.

Core MkDocs knows about the theme setting.

But Material decides what palette means.

Likewise:

theme:
  name: material
  features:
    - navigation.tabs

features is a Material configuration concept.

Therefore you cannot ask:

"What are all the possible theme keys in MkDocs?"

and get one universal list that applies to every theme.

The correct question is:

What does MkDocs define for the theme system, and what configuration does my chosen theme expose?

That's why the documentation seems fragmented.

docs.title: 13. Core MkDocs theme vocabulary
docs.text:
At the MkDocs level, the important configuration keys include:

theme:
  name: ...
  locale: ...
  custom_dir: ...
  static_templates: ...
  include_sidebar: ...

The exact supported options depend partly on the selected theme. MkDocs' own configuration documentation identifies name, locale, and custom_dir as core theme configuration concepts, while individual themes add their own options. (MkDocs)

docs.title: name
docs.text:
theme:
  name: material

Which installed theme?

Examples include:

theme:
  name: mkdocs

or:

theme:
  name: readthedocs

or, after installing Material:

theme:
  name: material

MkDocs currently ships with mkdocs and readthedocs built-in, while third-party themes can be installed separately. (MkDocs)

docs.title: 14. locale
docs.text:
theme:
  name: material
  language: en

Careful here: the exact key is theme-dependent.

Core MkDocs has:

theme:
  locale: en

Material has its own language configuration conventions/documentation.

This is another example of why you must distinguish core MkDocs configuration from Material's configuration vocabulary.

docs.title: 15. custom_dir
docs.text:
This is a core MkDocs mechanism for customizing/extending an existing theme.

For example:

theme:
  name: material
  custom_dir: overrides

That means:

"Use Material, but also look in my overrides directory for theme customizations."

MkDocs describes custom_dir as the directory containing files that override or supplement the parent theme. (MkDocs)

This is significantly more advanced than merely changing colors, but it is part of the actual theme system.

docs.title: PART III — NOW MATERIAL
docs.text:
Now your original question:

What the hell is primary? Is there a secondary? What is the exhaustive list?

Excellent question.

docs.title: 16. palette is Material's color configuration
docs.text:
Material gives you:

theme:
  name: material
  palette:
    primary: blue

palette means:

Configure the site's color palette.

Inside palette, Material currently gives you two major color roles:

palette:
  primary: ...
  accent: ...

There is not a standard:

secondary:

in Material's palette configuration.

The two principal configurable roles are:

primary
accent

Material documents them separately. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: 17. What is primary?
docs.text:
primary is the main color of the interface.

Material uses it for things including:

  • header
  • sidebar
  • text links
  • various other interface components

For example:

theme:
  name: material
  palette:
    primary: blue

means:

Make the site's primary theme color blue.

Material provides a predefined palette of names including:

red
pink
purple
deep purple
indigo
blue
light blue
cyan
teal
green
light green
lime
yellow
amber
orange
deep orange
brown
grey
blue grey
black
white

for primary. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: 18. What is accent?
docs.text:
accent is the color used for interactive/highlighted elements such as:

  • hovered links
  • buttons
  • scrollbars
  • other interactive elements

For example:

theme:
  name: material
  palette:
    primary: blue
    accent: orange

Conceptually:

BLUE
↓
main identity of site

ORANGE
↓
interactive/highlight emphasis

Material's documented accent choices are:

red
pink
purple
deep purple
indigo
blue
light blue
cyan
teal
green
light green
lime
yellow
amber
orange
deep orange

Notice that the accent palette is slightly different from the primary palette. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: 19. scheme
docs.text:
Now:

palette:
  scheme: default

This is not a color.

It specifies the color scheme.

Material currently provides:

default
slate

where:

default → light
slate   → dark

Material explicitly documents those two schemes. (GitHub Pages)

So:

palette:
  scheme: default
  primary: blue
  accent: orange

means:

PALETTE
│
├── scheme
│   └── light
│
├── primary
│   └── blue
│
└── accent
    └── orange

docs.title: 20. And this is why your original example was misleading
docs.text:
Someone giving you:

theme:
  name: material
  palette:
    scheme: default
    primary: blue

has effectively given you this:

theme
│
└── Material
    │
    └── palette
        │
        ├── scheme → light/dark scheme
        │
        ├── primary → main color
        │
        └── accent → interactive color

But they didn't explain the configuration vocabulary.

That's the part you were missing.

docs.title: PART IV — THE BIG MATERIAL theme MAP
docs.text:
Here's the useful mental map.

Material's theme: configuration is broadly divided into several areas.

theme:
│
├── name
│
├── language / localization
│
├── palette
│   ├── scheme
│   ├── primary
│   ├── accent
│   ├── media
│   └── toggle
│
├── font
│   ├── text
│   └── code
│
├── favicon
│
├── logo
│
├── icon
│
├── features
│   ├── navigation.*
│   ├── toc.*
│   ├── search.*
│   ├── content.*
│   ├── header.*
│   └── announce.*
│
├── custom_dir
│
└── other theme-specific configuration

Material's official setup documentation groups its configuration into areas including navigation, colors, fonts, icons/logo, search, header, footer, analytics, repository integration and other site behavior. (GitHub Pages)

That gives you the map.

Now let's go deeper into the two areas you're actually studying: navigation and theme configuration.

docs.title: PART V — MATERIAL'S NAVIGATION CONTROLS
docs.text:
Here's where another source of confusion comes in.

You have:

nav:

AND:

theme:
  features:
    - navigation.tabs

Those are not the same thing.

docs.title: nav
docs.text:
defines:

What the navigation contains.

docs.title: theme.features
docs.text:
defines:

How Material behaves/presents that navigation.

That's an enormous distinction.

docs.title: 21. navigation.tabs
docs.text:
theme:
  features:
    - navigation.tabs

This makes top-level navigation sections appear as tabs in Material's header area on sufficiently wide screens. (GitHub Pages)

Your:

nav:
  - Home: index.md
  - Guides:
      - Getting Started: getting-started.md
  - Reference:
      - YAML: yaml.md

defines:

Home
Guides
Reference

Then:

navigation.tabs

changes how those top-level navigation items are presented.

docs.title: 22. navigation.tabs.sticky
docs.text:
theme:
  features:
    - navigation.tabs
    - navigation.tabs.sticky

The tabs remain visible while scrolling. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: 23. navigation.sections
docs.text:
theme:
  features:
    - navigation.sections

Material renders top-level navigation sections as groups in the sidebar. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: 24. navigation.expand
docs.text:
theme:
  features:
    - navigation.expand

Expandable navigation sections are opened by default. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: 25. navigation.indexes
docs.text:
This one is particularly important.

Normally:

nav:
  - Guides:
      - Introduction: guides/index.md
      - Installation: guides/install.md

gives you a section and a separate introduction page.

With:

theme:
  features:
    - navigation.indexes

Material allows a section itself to have an index page. (GitHub Pages)

This is one of those features where nav and theme interact:

nav
↓
defines the structure

navigation.indexes
↓
changes how Material interprets/presents sections

docs.title: 26. navigation.top
docs.text:
theme:
  features:
    - navigation.top

Enables a back-to-top button when appropriate. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: 27. navigation.path
docs.text:
theme:
  features:
    - navigation.path

Adds breadcrumb-like navigation above the page title. (GitHub Pages)

Conceptually:

Guides → Configuration → YAML

# YAML Configuration

docs.title: 28. navigation.footer
docs.text:
theme:
  features:
    - navigation.footer

Enables previous/next navigation in the footer. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: 29. navigation.prune
docs.text:
theme:
  features:
    - navigation.prune

Material can render only the navigation items currently relevant/visible, reducing the HTML generated for large documentation sites. It is not compatible with navigation.expand. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: 30. The pattern should now be obvious
docs.text:
Instead of memorizing:

navigation.tabs
navigation.sections
navigation.expand
navigation.top
navigation.path
navigation.footer
navigation.indexes

read them literally:

navigation.tabs
        │
        └── tabs

navigation.sections
        │
        └── sections

navigation.expand
        │
        └── expansion

navigation.top
        │
        └── back-to-top

navigation.path
        │
        └── breadcrumb/path

navigation.footer
        │
        └── footer navigation

navigation.indexes
        │
        └── section index pages

This is the language of Material's configuration.

docs.title: PART VI — MATERIAL'S OTHER THEME CONTROLS
docs.text: Now let's make your original theme example genuinely useful.

docs.title: Colors
docs.text:
theme:
  name: material

  palette:
    scheme: default
    primary: blue
    accent: orange

docs.title: Dark mode
docs.text:
Material's dark scheme is:

theme:
  name: material

  palette:
    scheme: slate

Material also supports configuring multiple palette entries so users can switch between light and dark modes. (GitHub Pages)

For example:

theme:
  name: material

  palette:

    - scheme: default
      primary: blue
      accent: orange
      toggle:
        icon: material/brightness-7
        name: Switch to dark mode

    - scheme: slate
      primary: blue
      accent: orange
      toggle:
        icon: material/brightness-4
        name: Switch to light mode

Now palette has changed from a mapping into a list of palette configurations.

That's YAML.

And that's why understanding the structure matters.

docs.title: PART VII — FONTS
docs.text:
Material has:

theme:
  font:
    text: Roboto
    code: Roboto Mono

The conceptual model is:

font
├── text → normal documentation text
└── code → code/monospace text

Material supports a large set of Google Fonts and also allows self-hosted/custom fonts. (GitHub Pages)

You can also disable automatic Google Font loading:

theme:
  font: false

Material documents that as the way to fall back to system fonts rather than automatically loading fonts from Google. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: PART VIII — LOGO AND FAVICON
docs.text:
You can configure:

theme:
  logo: images/logo.png

and:

theme:
  favicon: images/favicon.png

Material's logo/icon documentation covers these and many other icon settings. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: PART IX — ICONS
docs.text:
Material has an icon configuration area.

For example:

theme:
  icon:
    previous: fontawesome/solid/angle-left
    next: fontawesome/solid/angle-right

The important conceptual distinction is:

logo
↓
brand/site logo

favicon
↓
browser tab icon

icon
↓
individual interface icons

Material provides a large icon set and allows many of the interface icons to be customized. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: PART X — FEATURES ARE SWITCHES
docs.text:
This is another thing that wasn't being explained properly.

When you see:

theme:
  features:
    - navigation.tabs
    - navigation.top
    - content.code.copy

don't interpret that as some mysterious YAML.

It's essentially:

features
↓
a list of switches

You're saying:

TURN ON
    navigation.tabs

TURN ON
    navigation.top

TURN ON
    content.code.copy

Material's feature flags are organized by component/function, which is why names such as navigation.tabs and navigation.instant exist. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: PART XI — THE REALLY IMPORTANT "EXHAUSTIVE" DISTINCTION
docs.text:
You asked:

"What is the exhaustive list of MkDocs or Material for MkDocs?"

There are two different exhaustive lists.

docs.title: List A — Core MkDocs
docs.text:
This is the configuration language understood by MkDocs itself.

The official MkDocs configuration reference is the authoritative list for that. (MkDocs)

Among its categories are things like:

Project information
├── site_name
├── site_url
├── repo_url
├── repo_name
└── ...

Documentation layout
├── nav
├── docs_dir
├── exclude_docs
├── draft_docs
└── not_in_nav

Theme
└── theme

Build directories
├── site_dir
├── ...
└── ...

Preview controls
├── watch
└── ...

Markdown extensions
├── markdown_extensions
└── ...

Plugins
└── plugins

Hooks
└── hooks

Extra files
├── extra_css
├── extra_javascript
└── extra_templates

That is MkDocs' configuration universe.

docs.title: List B — Material's theme configuration
docs.text:
Once you write:

theme:
  name: material

you're entering Material's configuration universe.

Material adds its own configuration vocabulary for things such as:

palette
font
icon
logo
favicon
features
language/localization
navigation behavior
search behavior
header behavior
footer behavior

Material's own setup documentation is therefore the authoritative reference for those. (GitHub Pages)

docs.title: THE WHOLE THING AS ONE MODEL
docs.text:
This is the model I want you to retain:

mkdocs.yml
│
├── nav
│   │
│   ├── pages
│   ├── sections
│   ├── nested sections
│   └── external links
│
└── theme
    │
    ├── MkDocs theme system
    │
    └── Material
        │
        ├── palette
        │   ├── scheme
        │   ├── primary
        │   ├── accent
        │   ├── media
        │   └── toggle
        │
        ├── font
        │   ├── text
        │   └── code
        │
        ├── logo
        ├── favicon
        │
        ├── icon
        │
        └── features
            │
            ├── navigation.tabs
            ├── navigation.sections
            ├── navigation.expand
            ├── navigation.indexes
            ├── navigation.top
            ├── navigation.path
            ├── navigation.footer
            ├── navigation.instant
            ├── navigation.tracking
            ├── navigation.prune
            └── ...

And now your original configuration:

theme:
  name: material
  palette:
    scheme: default
    primary: blue

is no longer a magical incantation.

You can read it:

theme
│
└── use Material
    │
    └── palette
        │
        ├── use light scheme
        │
        └── make blue the primary color

And if you wanted to construct your own:

theme:
  name: material

  palette:
    scheme: slate
    primary: deep purple
    accent: amber

  font:
    text: Roboto
    code: Roboto Mono

  features:
    - navigation.tabs
    - navigation.sections
    - navigation.expand
    - navigation.top
    - navigation.footer

you now have the semantic vocabulary to understand what every major line is doing.

docs.title: One final distinction that will save you a lot of confusion
docs.text:
There are three different kinds of "navigation" floating around:

1. nav:

MkDocs configuration

What pages/sections exist in my navigation, and in what hierarchy?

2. theme.features:
     - navigation.tabs

Material configuration

How should Material display/behave around that navigation?

3. toc

Table of contents

What headings exist inside the current Markdown page?

Those are three different systems.

If your page contains:

# YAML

## Scalars

## Sequences

## Mappings

that's the table of contents.

If mkdocs.yml contains:

nav:
  - YAML:
      - Basics: basics.md
      - Advanced: advanced.md

that's the site navigation.

And if you add:

theme:
  features:
    - navigation.tabs

that's Material changing the presentation/behavior of that site navigation.

That separation is the foundation for genuinely understanding nav and theme, rather than just copying configuration snippets.

docs.title: Mirror Mirror: Core Product & Architecture Blueprint
docs.text: Project Name: Mirror Mirror Tagline: The High-Fidelity Objective Performance Mirror Document Type: Core Architectural Blueprint & Product Master File Version: 1.0.0

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Traditional performance preparation (job interviews, auditions, sales calls, public speeches) is flawed. Practicing alone in front of a standard ("dumb") mirror creates double cognitive load: the brain must perform and evaluate simultaneously, making it blind to its own micro-behaviors. Practicing with peers introduces high friction, scheduling delays, and subjective bias.

docs.title: The Solution
docs.text: Mirror Mirror is an automated, multi-modal feedback loop powered by emergent AI (LLMs, Computer Vision, Speech-to-Text, Audio Waveform Analytics). It replaces passive reflection with an active, intelligent observer that measures, analyzes, and diagnoses physical and vocal performance in silence.

docs.title: The Non-Negotiable Core Philosophy: The MRI vs. The School
docs.text:
• Not a Teaching Platform: Mirror Mirror does not lecture, teach public speaking courses, or deliver theoretical lessons.
  • A High-Fidelity Diagnostic Tool (The MRI): Mirror Mirror exposes reality. It identifies blind spots and provides a clear, unvarnished mirror of how the user appears to the outside world.
  • The Diagnostic Prescription (Not Treatment): The system never instructs users on "how to live." It gives immediate, micro-targeted, actionable constraints (Prescriptions) designed to trigger a re-take (e.g., "Re-run this response in under 60 seconds").

docs.title: 1. Verbal Layer (What is said)
docs.text:
• Tech Engine: Speech-to-Text (e.g., Whisper API) mapped against scenario context.
  • Metrics Parsed: Logic structure (e.g., STAR framework), thematic relevance, vocabulary accuracy, narrative length.

docs.title: 2. Vocal Layer (How it is said)
docs.text:
• Tech Engine: Audio waveform processing tracking decibels, frequency variance, and WPM.
  • Metrics Parsed: Micro-acceleration spikes (rushing), pitch variations, filler word density ("like", "um", "uh"), monotone cadence.

docs.title: 3. Visual Layer (How it looks)
docs.text:
• Tech Engine: Computer Vision landmark tracking (e.g., MediaPipe) for face, eyes, and upper body.
  • Metrics Parsed: Eye-gaze vectors (camera lens vs. screen vs. drift), facial expression variance, fidgeting indicators, posture shifts.

docs.title: 3. The User Engagement Loop: Gamified Self-Awareness
docs.text:
Instead of relying on abstract long-term goals, Mirror Mirror engages users through an immediate, variable reward loop that turns self-correction into a sandbox.

+----------+      +-------------------+      +-----------------------+      +---------------+
|  1. SCAN | ---> | 2. DIAGNOSTIC REVEAL| ---> | 3. TARGETED PRESCRIPTION| ---> | 4. IMMEDIATE RE-SCAN |
+----------+      +-------------------+      +-----------------------+      +---------------+
  (Perform)       (Flagged Video Timeline)      (Specific Micro-Constraint)     (Chasing the Clean Scan)
  1. Scan: User records a short performance clip against a specific scenario prompt.
  2. Diagnostic Reveal: Interactive video timeline flagged with qualitative behavioral milestones (e.g., "Eye drift for 6s at 01:14").
  3. Targeted Prescription: AI issues a direct micro-constraint for the next attempt.
  4. Immediate Re-Scan: User retries immediately to remove the error flags and achieve a "Clean Scan."

docs.title: 4. Qualitative Data Translation Matrix
docs.text:
To avoid user anxiety caused by raw numbers, raw metrics are converted into qualitative human observations:

Telemetry (Raw Noise) Qualitative Observation (Clarity) Diagnostic Prescription WPM increased by 25% at 02:14 "You began rushing your words right when explaining why you left your last job." "Re-record this answer, but force yourself to pause for one full breath before stating your conclusion." Eye contact vector dropped to 40% "Your eyes drifted to the top-left corner whenever searching for a technical term." "Run a 30-second lightning round keeping your gaze locked directly on the camera lens." 8 filler word loops in 20s "You looped 'like' five times while defining your project workflow." "Microphone will mute for a split second every time a filler word is detected."

docs.title: 5. Target Demographics & Use Cases
docs.text:
Mirror Mirror rejects reliance on broken institutional gatekeepers (e.g., rigid university systems) and targets high-stakes independent performers:

  1. Job Seekers: Prepping for unscripted behavioral/technical interview panels.
  2. Remote Tech Freelancers: Pitching international clients on Zoom, mastering rate confidence and authoritative delivery.
  3. High-Ticket Sales Closers: Calibrating vocal tone to avoid sounding desperate or transactional during deal closings.
  4. Actors & Auditioners: Testing emotional variance, line delivery, script accuracy, and facial expression control.
  5. Content Creators & Podcasters: Eliminating stiff camera presence and mastering eye-contact dynamics.
  6. Immigrants & Global Professionals: Calibrating communication dynamics against regional corporate norms.

docs.title: 6. The "Vision Projection" Feature (The True Mirror)
docs.text:
A premium feature utilizing generative AI for Self-Modeling:

  • Input: User submits a baseline video and specifies a target persona (e.g., "Authoritative $150/hr tech consultant").
  • Generation: Generative video/audio pipelines synthesize the user's actual face and voice, programmatically removing posture slumps, vocal stutters, and eye-drift.

docs.title: The Core Concept: "The Smart Mirror"

If we want to build a truly "smart" mirror, the feedback cannot just be an analytics dashboard. It has to act like an empathetic, expert coach.

Here is how you can transform cold, noisy statistics into high-clarity, actionable guidance.

docs.title: 1. The "So What? + Now What?" Framework
docs.text:
Never show a statistic without immediately pairing it with its real-world impact (So What?) and a concrete, micro-actionable next step (Now What?).

Instead of treating the data as a grade, treat it as a symptom of an underlying behavior.

Example

❌ The Cold Stat (Noise): "Your speaking rate hit 180 WPM (a 20% spike) during the behavioral question."

Behavioral Translation (Clarity): "When you started talking about the conflict with your manager, you began rushing. • So What? It makes it harder for the interviewer to follow your logic, and it can signal nervousness. • Now What? Next time you feel yourself rushing, deliberately pause for one full breath before stating your final resolution. Let's practice just that sentence again."

docs.title: 2. Separate "Raw Data" from the "Primary Interface"
docs.text:

docs.title: 🟢 Celebrate (What to Keep Doing)
docs.text: • Example: "You nailed the introduction! Your eye contact was steady, and you sounded genuinely enthusiastic about the company culture."

docs.title: 🟡 Calibrate (The One Big Pivot)
docs.text: • Example: "Around the 2-minute mark, your answers started getting a bit long-winded. You lost the structure of your story. When you notice this happening, try to wrap up your point by tying it directly back to the original question."

docs.title: 🔵 Try This Right Now (Interactive Micro-Practice)
docs.text:
• Don't just give them a static report card. Give them a single, low-stakes prompt to try again immediately.
  • Example: "Let's re-do just the conclusion of that answer. Try to finish it in under three sentences. Ready when you are."

docs.title: 3. Humanize the AI’s Persona
docs.text:
Since you are using emergent LLMs, you can explicitly prompt the AI to adopt a coaching persona that understands the why behind human anxiety.

You can configure the AI interpreter to look for patterns rather than isolated blips: * Rushing $\rightarrow$ Interpret as: Adrenaline/Excitement/Anxiety. (Remedy: Grounding pauses). * Fidgeting/Looking away $\rightarrow$ Interpret as: Searching for words/Memory recall. (Remedy: Structuring thoughts with bullet points before speaking).

By shifting the language from measurement ("You failed this metric") to coaching ("Here is what your body language is communicating to the interviewer"), you remove the noise and replace it with genuine insight.

There is a massive, legitimate economy built around data collection, especially in the era of AI training. Let's break down exactly what data you can collect, how it can be used for the greater good, and how to monetize it legally and ethically without ever selling out your users.

docs.title: 1. What Data You Can Legitimately Collect
docs.text:
To keep user trust unbroken, you never collect or look at the substance of their private performance (e.g., you don't care about their specific job details or secrets). Instead, you collect Metadata and Anonymized Telemetry.

  • Vocal Biomarkers (Anonymized Audio Features): Pitch variations, speech cadence, and frequency shifts across different levels of anxiety. Crucial: You strip the actual spoken words (the transcript) and just keep the acoustic wave properties.
  • Micro-Expression and Landmark Telemetry: Coordinate maps of face movements (e.g., "At high cognitive load, the left eye consistently drifts 15 degrees left"). You don't save their actual video frames—you only save the mathematical vectors of the facial landmarks.
  • Anonymized Linguistics (The "Grammar Ghost"): Frequency of structural filler loops mapped to sentence lengths across various demographics.

docs.title: 2. Who Needs This Data Legitimately? (The Buyers)
docs.text:
There are entire industries starved for high-quality, real-world human behavioral telemetry to train their own systems. They don't want to know who the user is; they want to know how humans behave.

  • AI Model Developers (Speech & Vision Labs): Companies building the next generation of conversational AI or video avatars need highly accurate datasets on how people stutter, pause, use filler words, or move their eyes when they are nervous.
  • Enterprise HR Analytics Labs: Large companies trying to build internal assessment frameworks look for aggregate data on what separates an anxious, low-scoring speaker from a high-poise speaker.
  • EdTech and Virtual Reality Developers: Companies building corporate training simulations in VR need raw telemetry to make their AI bots look and react like realistic, nervous, or confident human beings.

docs.title: 3. How to Safely and Legitimately Monetize It
docs.text: You can make data a massive revenue stream for Mirror Mirror, but your business model must use one of these two airtight, modern frameworks to protect the platform's soul:

docs.title: Strategy A: The "Synthetic Data" Factory (Safest & Most Lucrative)
docs.text: Instead of selling your users' real audio or video vectors directly (which carries compliance liabilities under laws like GDPR or state biometric acts), you use your users' real telemetry to train a private generative AI model. * How it works: Your private model studies 100,000 anonymized sessions of anxious humans rushing their words. It then generates completely fake, 100% Synthetic Audio and Video Datasets that sound and look flawlessly human but belong to people who don't actually exist. * Why it's great: You can sell this synthetic training data to massive tech enterprises for millions of dollars. It contains zero personal identifiable information (PII), meaning you bypass severe biometric privacy restrictions entirely while monetizing the aggregate intelligence your platform gathered.

docs.title: Strategy B: The Opt-In "Data Dividend" (The Transparent Community)
docs.text: If you do decide to offer anonymized real text/audio metadata to research institutions, you make it a radical, transparent choice for the user. * The Feature: When a user signs up, you give them a toggle: "Allow Mirror Mirror to anonymize and license your vocal pacing metadata to help researchers study speech anxiety?" * The Incentive: If they toggle it ON, they get a "Data Dividend"—perhaps they get 5 free premium AI scans a month, or a discount on the marketplace we discussed. You turn data sharing into a mutual win, completely eliminating the "creepy, hidden surveillance" vibe.

docs.title: The Rule of Gold: Data Minimization
docs.text:
To build a sustainable platform, follow the modern principle of Data Minimization: The best way to protect your business from a data breach scandal is to never store raw data you don't actively need.

Run the vision and audio processing locally on the client's device or wipe the raw media servers every 24 hours. Keep only the math, the metadata, and the insights.

Google’s breakthrough was recognizing that Search Intent is the most valuable commodity on earth.

docs.title: The Core Engine: AdWords & AdSense (Released 2000–2003)
docs.text:
When you use a normal free app, advertisers pay to show you ads based on who you are (demographics). Google realized it is a million times more profitable to show ads based on what you want at this exact second.

docs.title: The Financial Mechanism: The Pay-Per-Click (PPC) Auction
docs.text: Google pioneered a system where advertisers don't pay just to show an ad; they only pay when a user actually clicks it. * The Auction: If five different laptop companies want to show up when you search "buy lightweight laptop," they enter a real-time, algorithmic auction. The company willing to pay the most per click gets the top slot. * The Scale: Because millions of high-intent searches happen every single second, those tiny clicks (ranging from $0.50 to $50+ per click depending on the industry) aggregate into billions of dollars of pure profit flowing into Google every single day—all while the front-facing search bar remains pristine, fast, and entirely free to the user.

Google’s algorithm instantly runs an auction in the milliseconds it takes to load the page: * They look at the top five shoe companies bidding for that exact keyword phase. * The company that wins the auction gets their link placed at the very top of the screen (the premium "real estate"). * The user clicks the link, buys the shoes, and Google charges that shoe company a fee for the click.

docs.title: 1. The "So What? + Now What?" Framework

Never show a statistic without immediately pairing it with its real-world impact (So What?) and a concrete, micro-actionable next step (Now What?).

• Now What? Next time you feel yourself rushing, deliberately pause for one full breath before stating your final resolution. Let's practice just that sentence again."

docs.title: 2. The Google Machinery: How a Free Tool Conquered the Earth
docs.text:
To understand how Google built a multi-billion-dollar empire while remaining completely free to the public, you have to look at the economic mechanism they invented in the early 2000s.

Before Google, search engines like Yahoo tried to make money like traditional magazines—by plastering massive, annoying banner ads all over the homepage. It was ugly and ineffective.

Google’s breakthrough was recognizing that Search Intent is the most valuable commodity on earth.

docs.title: The Core Engine: AdWords & AdSense (Released 2000–2003)
docs.text:
When you use a normal free app, advertisers pay to show you ads based on who you are (demographics). Google realized it is a million times more profitable to show ads based on what you want at this exact second.

If a user type into Google: "Best remote workspace setup" or "Reliable microphone for streaming," they are actively telling the world they are ready to spend money. Google didn't sell the user's data; they sold the real estate right above the organic search results to the highest bidder.

docs.title: The Financial Mechanism: The Pay-Per-Click (PPC) Auction
docs.text: Google pioneered a system where advertisers don't pay just to show an ad; they only pay when a user actually clicks it. * The Auction: If five different laptop companies want to show up when you search "buy lightweight laptop," they enter a real-time, algorithmic auction. The company willing to pay the most per click gets the top slot. * The Scale: Because millions of high-intent searches happen every single second, those tiny clicks (ranging from $0.50 to $50+ per click depending on the industry) aggregate into billions of dollars of pure profit flowing into Google every single day—all while the front-facing search bar remains pristine, fast, and entirely free to the user.
